value.body: Instead of a salaried job, some agriculture graduates run their own farm or agri-business, work with Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), or start ventures in inputs, advisory, processing or market linkage. Several government schemes support this with training, credit-linked subsidy and incubation. It is a self-employment path, so income depends on the venture.

items.label: 10,000 FPOs scheme
items.source: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (Parliament replies)

items.label: FPO equity grant
items.value: Up to ₹2,000 per farmer, max ₹15 lakh per FPO
items.source: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (Parliament replies)

items.label: Agri-Clinics & Agri-Business Centres
items.value: Subsidy on project cost up to ₹20 lakh (individual)
items.note: Training via MANAGE-linked institutes; subsidy routed through NABARD

value.title: How you get in
value.body: No exam. A degree in agriculture or allied subjects makes you eligible for the Agri-Clinics and Agri-Business Centres (ACABC) training and subsidy scheme. FPOs hire CEOs and staff directly, often through cluster-based business organisations. Agri-startups can apply to incubators under government programmes and agricultural universities.

value.title: At a glance
items: Weather, prices and working capital make income uneven, especially in the first few years.
Subsidies are back-ended and tied to bank loans, so you still need collateral or a strong project report.
FPO roles offer field experience in aggregation, marketing and input supply, but pay is often modest.
Many founders first work a few years in agri-business or extension to learn the market.
